questions.stem: On a supply and demand diagram, what does the vertical axis show?
questions.explanation: Price is always on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal one. Getting them the wrong way round makes every curve slope the wrong way, so it is worth fixing before anything else.

questions.stem: Why does the demand curve slope downwards?
options: People buy more when the price is lower
Producers make more when the price is lower
questions.explanation: Lower prices bring in buyers who would not pay more, so quantity demanded rises as price falls. That relationship is the whole reason the line slopes down.

questions.stem: Why does the supply curve slope upwards?
options: Producers will make more when the price is higher
Buyers want more when the price is higher
questions.explanation: A higher price makes production worth doing for more sellers, so quantity supplied rises with price. Supply and demand slope opposite ways, which is why they cross.

questions.stem: What does the point where the two curves cross show?
questions.explanation: At the crossing point the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers will provide. That is equilibrium — the market clears, with no shortage and no surplus.

questions.stem: The dashed lines from the crossing point to each axis show what?
options: The equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity
questions.explanation: They read the equilibrium off the axes: across to the price axis for P₁, down to the quantity axis for Q₁. Every conclusion in this topic is read off those two lines.

questions.stem: The diagram shows demand shifting to the right. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Follow the new crossing point to each axis: price rises and quantity rises. A demand shift to the right is an increase in demand, and the supply curve has not moved.

questions.stem: Which change would shift demand to the right, as the diagram shows?
options: A change in the price of ice cream itself
Nothing — the curve moves on its own
A heatwave makes more people want ice cream
A change that shifts supply instead
questions.explanation: A heatwave makes more people want ice cream is a demand factor, so it moves the demand curve to the right. A change in the price of ice cream itself would move *along* a curve rather than shift it, which is the distinction this topic turns on.

questions.stem: After demand shifts right, what is true at the original price?
options: The quantity supplied always equals the quantity demanded
The market is no longer in equilibrium, so price adjusts
Nothing changes until the government intervenes
questions.explanation: At the old price the two quantities no longer match — there is a shortage. Price moves until they match again, which is what takes the market to the new crossing point.

questions.stem: The diagram shows demand shifting to the left. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Follow the new crossing point to each axis: price falls and quantity falls. A demand shift to the left is an decrease in demand, and the supply curve has not moved.

questions.stem: Which change would shift demand to the left, as the diagram shows?
options: A change in the price of ice cream itself
Nothing — the curve moves on its own
A cold snap means fewer people want ice cream
A change that shifts supply instead
questions.explanation: A cold snap means fewer people want ice cream is a demand factor, so it moves the demand curve to the left. A change in the price of ice cream itself would move *along* a curve rather than shift it, which is the distinction this topic turns on.

questions.stem: After demand shifts left, what is true at the original price?
options: The market is no longer in equilibrium, so price adjusts
Nothing changes until the government intervenes
The quantity supplied always equals the quantity demanded
questions.explanation: At the old price the two quantities no longer match — there is a surplus. Price moves until they match again, which is what takes the market to the new crossing point.

questions.stem: The diagram shows supply shifting to the right. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Follow the new crossing point to each axis: price falls and quantity rises. A supply shift to the right is an increase in supply, and the demand curve has not moved.

questions.stem: Which change would shift supply to the right, as the diagram shows?
options: A new machine lets factories make ice cream more cheaply
A change that shifts demand instead
A change in the price of ice cream itself
Nothing — the curve moves on its own
questions.explanation: A new machine lets factories make ice cream more cheaply is a supply factor, so it moves the supply curve to the right. A change in the price of ice cream itself would move *along* a curve rather than shift it, which is the distinction this topic turns on.

questions.stem: After supply shifts right, what is true at the original price?
options: The quantity supplied always equals the quantity demanded
The market is no longer in equilibrium, so price adjusts
Nothing changes until the government intervenes
questions.explanation: At the old price the two quantities no longer match — there is a surplus. Price moves until they match again, which is what takes the market to the new crossing point.

questions.stem: The diagram shows supply shifting to the left. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Follow the new crossing point to each axis: price rises and quantity falls. A supply shift to the left is an decrease in supply, and the demand curve has not moved.

questions.stem: Which change would shift supply to the left, as the diagram shows?
options: Nothing — the curve moves on its own
The price of milk rises sharply
A change that shifts demand instead
A change in the price of ice cream itself
questions.explanation: The price of milk rises sharply is a supply factor, so it moves the supply curve to the left. A change in the price of ice cream itself would move *along* a curve rather than shift it, which is the distinction this topic turns on.

questions.stem: After supply shifts left, what is true at the original price?
options: The quantity supplied always equals the quantity demanded
The market is no longer in equilibrium, so price adjusts
Nothing changes until the government intervenes
questions.explanation: At the old price the two quantities no longer match — there is a shortage. Price moves until they match again, which is what takes the market to the new crossing point.

questions.stem: The price of ice cream falls and people buy more. What does the diagram show?
options: A movement along the demand curve, not a shift
questions.explanation: A change in the price of the good itself moves you *along* a curve. Only something else — weather, incomes, the price of milk — shifts the whole curve. This is the single most tested distinction in the topic.

questions.stem: Incomes rise across the country. What happens in the ice cream market?
options: Nothing, because ice cream prices have not changed
Demand shifts right, raising price and quantity
Demand shifts left, lowering price and quantity
questions.explanation: Higher incomes mean people buy more at every price, which is a shift of the whole demand curve to the right. Price and quantity both rise.

questions.stem: A new tax on ice cream producers raises their costs. What happens?
options: Supply shifts left, raising price and lowering quantity
Nothing, because the tax is paid by producers
questions.explanation: Higher costs mean less is supplied at every price, so supply shifts left. Price rises and quantity falls — and buyers end up bearing part of a tax charged to producers, which is worth noticing.

questions.stem: In the petrol market, an oil shortage cuts the amount refineries can supply. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Supply shifts left: price rises, quantity falls
Supply shifts right: price falls, quantity rises
questions.explanation: The same reasoning works in any market: an oil shortage cuts the amount refineries can supply, so the supply curve moves left. Reading the new crossing point gives price rises and quantity falls.

questions.stem: In the housing market, a growing population means more people looking to buy. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Demand shifts right: price rises, quantity rises
Demand shifts left: price falls, quantity falls
questions.explanation: The same reasoning works in any market: a growing population means more people looking to buy, so the demand curve moves right. Reading the new crossing point gives price rises and quantity rises.

questions.stem: In the laptops market, cheaper components lower the cost of building each laptop. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Supply shifts right: price falls, quantity rises
Supply shifts left: price rises, quantity falls
questions.explanation: The same reasoning works in any market: cheaper components lower the cost of building each laptop, so the supply curve moves right. Reading the new crossing point gives price falls and quantity rises.

questions.stem: In the concert tickets market, the band's popularity fades and fewer people want to go. What does the diagram show happening?
options: Demand shifts left: price falls, quantity falls
Demand shifts right: price rises, quantity rises
questions.explanation: The same reasoning works in any market: the band's popularity fades and fewer people want to go, so the demand curve moves left. Reading the new crossing point gives price falls and quantity falls.
